Reading both sides of the 'holism vs reductionism' is interesting. Reductionism is making a big surge right now, and I think that it has to do with the burden of proof, basically. If there is an explanatory gap (holism), then we need to grope around in the dark to figure out what the magical 'special sauce' is that differentiates a conscious information system from an unconscious one. If there is no explanatory gap, though (reductionism), we can build the best approximations of the conscious model that we have, on hardware that we have, and we can turn them on and ask them questions.

I don't think even the creation of a human-intelligence artifact that behaves sentiently will settle this argument. There will be people that argue that the machines have become conscious (reductionists), and those that say that they're automatons that are very detailed mimics of things that are actually conscious (holists).

Myself, I like to think that holism is correct and that the 'special sauce' is of quantum-mechanical origin. I like the idea that systems which generate consciousness depend on the way that quantum superpositions collapse into seemingly 'random' states. I even have such silly armchair-philosopher ideas as, 'conscious agents select which location a superposition collapses to, but they must obey the probabilities in the long run to preserve entropy'--embarrassing to say to a mathematician, but a lot of fun to contemplate on my own.
